title: Injury and Regeneration: Why the Brain Does Not Regrow

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: The long process that carries a neuron's output is the {{c1::axon}}.
cards.back: The cell body holds the nucleus and makes most of the cell's proteins.
cards.quote: The axon is the long process that carries a neuron's output

cards.front: After an axon is cut, the {{c1::distal}} piece is separated from its cell body.
cards.back: The proximal piece remains attached and may grow a new tip.
cards.quote: The distal piece, beyond the cut, is separated from its cell body.

cards.front: For a mature mammalian axon cut while its cell body survives, what governs whether the attached piece regrows?
cards.back: Regrowth tends to occur when the neuron's drive to grow outweighs resistance from surrounding tissue.
cards.why: Drive and resistance are a rule of thumb, not measured quantities.
cards.quote: The piece still attached tends to regrow where the neuron's drive to grow outweighs the resistance of the tissue around it.

cards.front: Breakdown of the distal stump after axon injury is called {{c1::Wallerian degeneration}}.
cards.back: It occurs in peripheral nerves and in the brain and spinal cord.
cards.quote: Breakdown of the distal stump is still called Wallerian degeneration.

cards.front: Design a gene-deletion experiment that would support an active destruction program in severed axons rather than simple loss of supplies.
cards.back: Cut axons in candidate-gene knockout and normal neurons. If knockout distal stumps remain intact for weeks while normal stumps fragment within days, the deleted gene supports active destruction.
cards.why: The test rests on the rule that removing a required program component can stop destruction even though the stump remains cut off from its cell body.
cards.quote: A program has parts, and removing a part should stop it.

cards.front: A whole-animal gene deletion preserves severed axons. How could you test whether protection comes from the neurons themselves rather than glia or immune cells?
cards.back: Cut mutant-neuron axons in culture without glia or immune cells, or delete the gene only in neurons. Continued protection supports a neuronal action.
cards.quote: cut the axons of mutant neurons in culture, away from glia and immune cells, or delete the gene only in neurons.

cards.front: How do Wlds and Sarm1 deletion provide different kinds of evidence about axon degeneration?
cards.back: Wlds adds a protective fusion protein; deleting Sarm1 removes a normal program component. Protection after deletion shows that normal degeneration requires an active mechanism.
cards.quote: Deleting one ordinary gene gave protection like that of the odd fusion.
cards.section: The slow mouse, and a knockout that copies it

cards.front: The NMNAT isoform that works in axons is {{c1::NMNAT2}}.
cards.back: It uses NMN and the adenylyl part of ATP to make NAD+.
cards.quote: NMNAT2 is the NMNAT isoform that works in axons.
cards.section: The program: a switch that waits for the deliveries to stop

cards.front: Why does NMNAT2 decline in a severed distal axon before the axon fragments?
cards.back: NMNAT2 is short-lived and needs constant replacement from the cell body. Cutting the axon stops those deliveries while existing NMNAT2 continues to be lost.
cards.quote: After a cut the deliveries stop, and NMNAT2 in the stump falls below a threshold before the axon breaks up.
cards.section: The program: a switch that waits for the deliveries to stop

cards.front: In the leading model, how does loss of NMNAT2 activate SARM1?
cards.back: NMN accumulates as NAD+ falls. The rising NMN-to-NAD+ ratio favours NMN binding to the ARM sensor domain and switches SARM1 on.
cards.why: NMN supply and NAD+ use also affect the ratio; it is not determined by NMNAT2 alone.
cards.quote: In the leading model, NMN competes for the same site, and a rise in NMN relative to NAD+ switches SARM1 on.
cards.section: The program: a switch that waits for the deliveries to stop

cards.front: The TIR enzyme domain of SARM1 cleaves {{c1::NAD+}}.
cards.back: NAD+ falls rapidly, followed by ATP.
cards.quote: The TIR domain of SARM1, its enzyme part, cleaves NAD+.
cards.section: The program: a switch that waits for the deliveries to stop

cards.front: An injured axon loses much of its NAD+, followed by ATP. What happens to intracellular calcium and axon structure, and why?
cards.back: Calcium rises and the axon fragments. Energy failure is followed by calcium elevation, which activates proteases that cut the cytoskeleton.
cards.quote: As energy fails, calcium rises inside the axon.
cards.section: The program: a switch that waits for the deliveries to stop

cards.front: How do calpains turn the calcium rise in an injured axon into fragmentation?
cards.back: Calcium activates calpains, which are proteases that cut the cytoskeleton, allowing the axon to fragment.
cards.quote: Calpains, proteases switched on by calcium, cut the cytoskeleton, and the axon fragments
cards.section: The program: a switch that waits for the deliveries to stop

cards.front: A severed mouse axon contains the Wlds protein. Predict the effect on degeneration and explain its position in the NMNAT2–SARM1 sequence.
cards.back: Degeneration is delayed: Wlds supplies longer-lived NMNAT activity upstream of SARM1, maintaining the protective activity after deliveries from the cell body stop.
cards.quote: The Wlds protein works because it is a longer-lived source of NMNAT activity that keeps the handle pressed after the cut.
cards.section: The program: a switch that waits for the deliveries to stop

cards.front: Cut Sarm1-null sensory axons resist degeneration. Normal SARM1 restores NAD+ loss and fragmentation, but a version unable to cleave NAD+ restores neither. What does this comparison establish?
cards.back: SARM1's NAD+-cleaving activity is required for degeneration in this experiment; merely supplying the SARM1 protein is insufficient.
cards.quote: The TIR domain of SARM1, its enzyme part, cleaves NAD+.
cards.section: The program: a switch that waits for the deliveries to stop

cards.front: Developing mice lacking NMNAT2 have stalled axons and die around birth; deleting Sarm1 as well rescues axon growth and survival. What causal ordering follows, and what timing question remains open?
cards.back: NMNAT2 loss acts through SARM1: removing the downstream executioner rescues loss of the upstream supply. This developmental rescue does not determine the latent-phase duration in a cut mature nerve.
cards.why: This rests on downstream deletion rescuing an upstream defect, combined with the distinction between developing axons and the mature-axon injury rule.
cards.quote: Removing the switch rescues axons that lack the delivery, so losing the delivery works by tripping the switch.
cards.section: The program: a switch that waits for the deliveries to stop

cards.front: Why is injury-induced distal-stump degeneration distinct from whole-cell apoptosis?
cards.back: It can proceed locally without a nucleus and despite blocked or missing caspases. By contrast, developmental trophic-factor-deprivation pruning requires caspases.
cards.quote: Injury-induced degeneration of the stump proceeds when caspases are blocked or missing, while the developmental pruning of axons deprived of trophic factor needs them.
cards.section: The program: a switch that waits for the deliveries to stop

cards.front: How do repair Schwann cells make an injured peripheral nerve more favourable for regrowth?
cards.back: They help break down myelin, recruit blood macrophages to clear debris, and form tubes that guide regrowing axons toward their targets.
cards.quote: they help break down myelin, they recruit macrophages from the blood to clear the rest

cards.front: Debris clearance in a peripheral nerve is slowed while the proximal axon remains able to grow. Must regrowth stop until every fragment is removed, and why?
cards.back: No. Clearance helps open the path, but regrowth can overlap with it; complete debris removal is not a prerequisite for growth to start.
cards.quote: Clearing helps a new axon use the path, though regrowth need not wait for it to finish.

cards.front: The motile tip formed by a regrowing proximal axon is a {{c1::growth cone}}.
cards.quote: The proximal stump forms a growth cone, the motile tip that leads a growing axon.
cards.section: The attached piece: drive against resistance

cards.front: What does improved central-branch regrowth after an earlier peripheral-branch injury show in a dorsal root ganglion sensory neuron?
cards.back: The neuron's growth state can be raised by the peripheral injury. The central environment alone cannot explain the outcome.
cards.quote: cutting the peripheral branch before the central branch is injured raises the central branch's regrowth.
cards.section: The attached piece: drive against resistance

cards.front: Adult rat central axons grow along a peripheral nerve bridge but stop shortly after leaving it for central tissue. Which explanation of poor central regrowth does this challenge?
cards.back: It challenges the claim that all adult central neurons have irreversibly lost the ability to extend axons. A peripheral path permits some regrowth, implicating the surroundings.
cards.quote: Some adult central neurons can regrow when the path is peripheral; their central surroundings do much to stop them.

cards.front: PTEN normally acts as a brake on the {{c1::mTOR}} pathway that promotes protein synthesis and cell growth.
cards.quote: PTEN is a brake on the mTOR pathway, the kinase pathway that drives protein synthesis and cell growth.

cards.front: What did increased optic-nerve regrowth after PTEN deletion in mouse retinal ganglion cells establish about intrinsic growth?
cards.back: Intrinsic growth limits regrowth: changing the neurons allowed far more axons than normal to regenerate despite central surroundings. The regrowing axons came from a minority of neurons.
cards.quote: Axons regenerated through the crushed optic nerve, with the central surroundings left in place.

cards.front: Taken together, do peripheral nerve grafts and neuronal PTEN deletion support two mandatory gates that must both open before central axons regrow? Explain the inference and its limits.
cards.back: They support a balance, not two mandatory gates: each produced growth while changing mainly one side. Grafts also signal to neurons, and PTEN loss also improves survival, so neither isolates one factor perfectly.
cards.why: The inference combines regrowth after changing mainly the tissue with regrowth after changing mainly the neuron.
cards.quote: Neither is a gate that must open first, since each experiment got growth while changing mainly one side

cards.front: Nogo-66, MAG and OMgp bind the growth-cone receptor {{c1::NgR}}.
cards.back: Partner proteins transmit the signal to RhoA, leading to growth-cone collapse.
cards.quote: all bind the Nogo receptor, NgR, on the growth cone

cards.front: Which matrix molecules with long sugar chains are abundant around a central nervous system lesion?
cards.back: Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, produced by reactive astrocytes and other cells, including NG2 glia.
cards.quote: the lesion is rich in chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, matrix proteins with long sugar chains

cards.front: Why does improved axon growth after chondroitinase ABC treatment in spinal-cord-injured rats implicate lesion proteoglycans?
cards.back: The enzyme digests their sugar chains. Improved growth after this treatment supports those chains contributing to resistance at the lesion.
cards.quote: Digesting their sugar chains with the bacterial enzyme chondroitinase ABC improved axon growth and recovery in rats with spinal cord injury.

cards.front: In a mouse spinal cord lesion receiving growth-promoting treatment, the astrocyte border is also removed. Predict the effect on stimulated regrowth and explain.
cards.back: Stimulated regrowth falls. The border also supports growth; removing it reduced treatment-stimulated regrowth in mice.
cards.quote: it reduced regrowth that had been stimulated with growth-promoting treatments.

cards.front: What protective role does the scar around a central nervous system injury serve?
cards.back: It limits the spread of damage.
cards.quote: The scar also limits the spread of damage, so the aim is to change it, not remove it.

cards.front: Deleting Nogo, MAG and OMgp in mice removes real growth-cone inhibitors. Must this produce substantial regeneration of cut central axons? Explain.
cards.back: No. Little or no extra regeneration may occur because other barriers remain and most neurons may still have insufficient growth drive. Spared fibres may instead sprout more.
cards.quote: Myelin inhibitors are one barrier among several, and the others remain.
cards.section: Why each fix is only partial

cards.front: In a hypothetical group of 100 neurons, 1 regrows at baseline, 2 after lowering resistance, 10 after raising drive, and 16 after both. How much does the combined gain exceed the sum of separate gains?
cards.back: Separate gains: (2 − 1) + (10 − 1) = 10 neurons. Combined gain: 16 − 1 = 15 neurons. Excess combined gain: 15 − 10 = 5 neurons.
cards.why: These are illustrative settings, not experimental counts or a prediction of clinical success.
cards.quote: In this model, both add about 15.
cards.section: Why each fix is only partial

cards.front: A conceptual model says axons regrow when growth drive exceeds tissue resistance. Why might raising drive and lowering resistance together help more than either alone, yet fail to guarantee a more-than-additive gain?
cards.back: Both changes can bring more neurons past the threshold. The size of the combined gain depends on the spread of growth drive and the size of each change; gains can exceed, equal, or fall below a simple sum.
cards.why: This combines the drive-versus-resistance rule with the threshold model. Its numbers are illustrative, so it motivates testing combinations rather than guaranteeing success.
cards.quote: With a different spread, or with changes large enough to reach most neurons, the gains might only add, or add up to less.
cards.section: Why each fix is only partial

cards.front: Why is axon regrowth across an injury insufficient evidence of useful functional recovery?
cards.back: The axon must also reach the right target and form working connections. Extension alone establishes neither.
cards.quote: Useful function returns only when a regrowing axon reaches the right target and forms working connections

cards.front: Assume a peripheral axon has 50 mm to regrow, starts after a 20-day delay, and then advances steadily at 1 mm/day. When does it reach the target after injury?
cards.back: Growth time = 50 mm ÷ (1 mm/day) = 50 days. Total time = 20 days + 50 days = 70 days after injury.
cards.why: The delay and steady speed are assumptions for this calculation; actual growth rates depend on the nerve and injury.
cards.quote: An axon regrows at around a millimetre a day.

cards.front: Two peripheral axons start regrowing at the same speed, but one has much farther to travel. Why can the longer route reduce recovery even if growth begins normally?
cards.back: The longer route takes more time, and the Schwann-cell repair state may fade before regrowth reaches the target. Some axons may never reconnect.
cards.quote: the repair state of Schwann cells does not last as long as slow regrowth over a long distance needs

cards.front: Why can preserving a fully severed distal axon for weeks fail to restore its function?
cards.back: Preservation does not reconnect it to its cell body. Recovery requires the attached axon to regrow to the right target and form working connections.
cards.quote: A fully severed stump cannot rejoin its cell body on its own however long it survives

cards.front: In the NMNAT2–SARM1 model, compare adding an NAD+ precursor to a cut stump before versus after NMNAT2 is lost. Why might the effect change?
cards.back: While NMNAT remains, precursor-derived NMN can become NAD+. After NMNAT2 loss, extra NMN could instead raise the NMN-to-NAD+ ratio and promote SARM1 activation; benefit is not assured.
cards.why: This combines precursor conversion through NMN with the ratio-sensing model. Delivery and amount matter, and the adverse effect is a possibility, not a guaranteed outcome.
cards.quote: Once the stump has lost NMNAT2, extra NMN could add to the signal that switches SARM1 on.

cards.front: Design a comparison testing whether SARM1 inhibition after complete axon severing preserves axons or actually restores useful connections. Which outcomes would distinguish those claims?
cards.back: Compare treated and control injuries. Score distal-stump survival separately from proximal regrowth to the correct target and working connections. More intact distal axons alone supports preservation, not restored connectivity.
cards.why: The design combines the separate degeneration and regrowth programs with the requirement that functional recovery needs correct target reconnection.
cards.quote: The two fates need different fixes.

cards.front: In the Deppmann laboratory's mouse-neuron injury cultures, was spheroid rupture alone sufficient to commit Sarm1-null axons to catastrophic degeneration? Explain the evidence.
cards.back: No. Spheroids ruptured while the axons resisted degeneration, showing rupture alone was insufficient. The proposed ordering from this laboratory's culture work remains a model.
cards.quote: rupture alone does not commit an axon, since Sarm1-null axons rupture spheroids and still resist degeneration.
